1.pericope_label: Thou also, son of man, take thee a tile, and lay it before thee, and pourtray upon it the city, even Jerusalem: And lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about. Moreover take thou unto thee an iron pan, and set it for a wall of iron between thee and the city: and set thy face against it, and it shall be besieged, and thou shalt lay siege against it. This shall be a sign to the house of Israel.

schools.summary: Ellicott confirms from the buried libraries of Babylonia and Nineveh that drawing on clay tiles was ordinary practice, but reading the whole run of these chapters concludes that the acts were described rather than performed, prefers a flat baking plate to a pan and takes it for the strength of the besieging lines and the impossibility of breaking out by a sally, asks how likely a fresh siege can have looked when Egypt was beaten and the country already three times conquered so that only a fresh revolt could bring the armies back, and explains that the house of Israel here means the whole nation, Judah standing for what the earlier deportations had left.

Gill prefers a green unbaked brick as easier to cut, canvasses the reasons offered for the material and settles on the Babylonian habit of writing on tiles, and collects readings of the iron plate without choosing between the hardness of the people's hearts, the miseries of captivity and the settled anger of God; Calvin sketches ancient siegecraft, mounds thrown up to fill trenches and wooden towers moved forward, notes that firearms made such machines obsolete, and turns the whole scene into an argument that a sacrament is distinguished from an empty show by nothing but the word of God, applying the rule sharply to the ceremonies of Rome.

Clarke insists the object is a brick and not a roof tile, citing an ancient authority for dimensions of two feet by one and four inches thick, and stops on the battering ram as first mentioned here, a beam headed with brass slung on ropes and hauled back by a gang, absent from the siege of Troy and reappearing later in a Carthaginian siege; Wesley reduces the command to drawing a map, and transfers the hardness of the iron to the besiegers' patience.

Henry contrasts a city once engraved on the divine palms, its tribal names cut in precious stones on a priest's breastplate, with one now worth only a brittle piece of clay laid where the eye can work on the heart, and finds in the iron plate an obstinacy on both sides, invaders resolved never to withdraw and defenders resolved never to capitulate.

debates.question: What does the iron plate signify?

positions.position: The strength of the besieging lines and the impossibility of escape by a sally.
Obstinacy on both sides of it, invaders resolved never to withdraw and defenders never to capitulate.
The resolution and patience of the besiegers.
Various: the hardness of the people's hearts and the blackness of their sins, or the miseries of the captivity, or the settled anger of God.

outliers.claim: Argues from the commanded sign that a sacrament is distinguished from an empty show by nothing but the word of God, and applies the rule against ceremonies devised to dazzle the simple.
Takes the battering ram to be first mentioned in this verse, noting its absence from the siege of Troy and its later appearance in a Carthaginian siege.

themes: Thou also, son of man, take thee a tile, and lay it before thee, and pourtray upon it the city, even Jerusalem:
And lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about.

4.pericope_label: Lie thou also upon thy left side, and lay the iniquity of the house of Israel upon it: according to the number of the days that thou shalt lie upon it thou shalt bear their iniquity. For I have laid upon thee the years of their iniquity, according to the number of the days, three hundred and ninety days: so shalt thou bear the iniquity of the house of Israel. And when thou hast accomplished them, lie again on thy right side, and thou shalt bear the iniquity of the house of Judah forty days: I have appointed thee each day for a year. Therefore thou shalt set thy face toward the siege of Jerusalem, and thine arm shall be uncovered, and thou shalt prophesy against it. And, behold, I will lay bands upon thee, and thou shalt not turn thee from one side to another, till thou hast ended the days of thy siege.

schools.summary: Ellicott explains that to bear the iniquity of another is a standing expression for suffering the punishment due to sin, so the prophet stands for the people under judgment, and states candidly that this sits oddly beside his standing also for the besiegers, adding that such inconsistencies are common in symbolic action and spoil nothing; he distinguishes the two houses expressly, explains the left side as the north because the Oriental takes his bearings facing east, reads the set face as steadfast purpose and a favourite phrase of this prophet, takes the bared arm as made ready for battle, and hears in the bands a judgment from which not pity only but weariness was to be shut out.

Gill sets out both cases on whether the lying was real or seen and calls neither contemptible, urging that nobody could lie so long without a miracle and that a later dated notice leaves too few days, records the further question whether the forty fall inside the longer count, and takes the bands for the besiegers held to their work rather than the besieged, an emblem of an unalterable decree; Calvin finds the purpose in opposing a people who thought themselves punished beyond their deserts, which he calls the habit of hypocrites who grumble at severity and offer something by way of composition, notes that those spared had grown the more stubborn while the deportees complained, describes the coat pulled half off to free one arm, and admits the performance would be frigid were the meaning not attached to the figure.

Clarke has no doubt the acts were performed, the man chained to a couch for three hundred and ninety days and then forty, and supplies a key in which the prophet stands for the nation, his lying for its prostration, his bonds for its helplessness, and the days for years, the longer term marking both the siege and the exile; he reports a reckoning that sums the idolatrous portions of six reigns to make exactly forty years; Wesley reads the number as measuring both how long the offence was endured and how long the penalty would run, starts the longer count at a king's lapse into idolatry, and counts the forty from a covenant renewal to the temple's destruction.

debates.question: Were the symbolic acts performed or only seen in vision?

positions.position: Performed: he lay chained to a couch for the full terms.
The reasons on both sides are respectable; nobody could lie so long without a miracle, and a later dated notice leaves too few days.

debates.question: What do the forty days measure?

positions.position: The idolatrous portions of six reigns, which sum to exactly forty years; or else the time taken to sack the city and temple.
The period from a covenant renewal to the temple's destruction, through which punishment was deferred.

outliers.claim: Concedes that the prophet represents both the punished people and the besiegers who punish them, and answers that such inconsistencies are common in symbolic action and mar nothing.
Finds the purpose of the sign in the pride of people who thought themselves punished beyond their deserts, those spared at home having grown the more stubborn for being spared.

9.pericope_label: Take thou also unto thee wheat, and barley, and beans, and lentiles, and millet, and fitches, and put them in one vessel, and make thee bread thereof, according to the number of the days that thou shalt lie upon thy side, three hundred and ninety days shalt thou eat thereof. And thy meat which thou shalt eat shall be by weight, twenty shekels a day: from time to time shalt thou eat it. Thou shalt drink also water by measure, the sixth part of an hin: from time to time shalt thou drink. And thou shalt eat it as barley cakes, and thou shalt bake it with dung that cometh out of man, in their sight. And the Lord said, Even thus shall the children of Israel eat their defiled bread among the Gentiles, whither I will drive them. Then said I, Ah Lord God! behold, my soul hath not been polluted: for from my youth up even till now have I not eaten of that which dieth of itself, or is torn in pieces; neither came there abominable flesh into my mouth. Then he said unto me, Lo, I have given thee cow’s dung for man’s dung, and thou shalt prepare thy bread therewith. Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, behold, I will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem: and they shall eat bread by weight, and with care; and they shall drink water by measure, and with astonishment: That they may want bread and water, and be astonied one with another, and consume away for their iniquity.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the grains run from best to worst so that every kind would be sought, that mixing them in one vessel violated at least the spirit of the law, and that only the longer term is named though the rule must have covered both; he computes the ration from a heavier shekel at under eleven ounces and calls it scarcely enough to live on, observes that food weighed rather than measured is itself the mark of scarcity, shifts the offence of the fuel from the physical to the ceremonial, answers the argument that doing it in their sight proves a real act by making the public performance part of what was seen, and states that the law had fenced the people so thoroughly that exile must defile them.

Gill notes that only the first two grains were ever human bread, computes the twenty shekels at ten ounces from an ancient historian's half-ounce shekel, has the cakes baked under ashes that are neither wood nor straw nor turf, and records that the prayer was heard and the terms eased; Calvin grades the scale of want from wheat through barley and vetches to lentils and millet, marks the failure of water as the last stage of famine, insists the objection to the fuel was not palate but lawfulness, and distinguishes two punishments in the broken staff of bread, since even a sufficient supply may be robbed of strength.

Clarke recognises the practice of eking out finer grain with coarser, turns the stock into three hundred and ninety daily loaves with water at a pint and a half, explains that dried dung is ordinary fuel in the East and offers the mitigation that it never touched the bread but only heated the plate, and matches the years back to the reign in which national idolatry began and the days to the siege less the months the besiegers spent away; Wesley says all the grain will be little enough, calls the acts a vision, and closes on the symmetry that those who would not serve God cheerfully in plenty were made to serve enemies in want.
Henry calls the mixture what horses and hogs are fed, and compares the sack to a beggar's bag filled a handful at a time from different doors.

debates.question: How bad is the defilement of the fuel?

positions.position: Much less than it appears, since the fuel never touched the bread but only heated the plate the cakes lay on.
Not a matter of disgust at all but of ceremonial law, cakes baked in hot ashes taking defilement from the fuel.
Not the palate but lawfulness: a man who had fed carelessly all his life could not have prayed against it as this one did.

outliers.claim: Meets the strongest objection to reading the chapter as vision, that the act was done in their sight, by making the public performance itself part of what was seen.
Offers a mitigation of the fuel's horror on the ground that it heated only the plate beneath the cakes and never touched the bread.
